The foundations were laid by people asking questions about how the immune system distinguishes self from non-self, with no clinical product in mind. Jacques Miller's neonatal thymectomy experiments in the early 1960s established that T cells were a distinct lineage derived from the thymus. Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty then showed, using a lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus model, that cytotoxic T cells could only kill infected target cells sharing the same MHC haplotype — the finding called MHC restriction, which established that T cells read an antigen-MHC complex as a single unit rather than reading antigen alone.

The paper's explanation is pharmacological rather than immunological, and it rests on where the cytokines went. Blood levels of IL-15 peaked immediately after lymphodepletion and then stayed low. IL-21 rose modestly and peaked in the second week. Both remained low systemically throughout. Yet the engineered cells expanded to a peak at week two and produced a response. The authors' reading is that autocrine and paracrine signalling — cytokine acting on the cell that made it and on its neighbours — drove a therapeutic level of expansion locally, without generating the systemic exposure that causes cytokine release syndrome.

For almost nobody reading this, no. The in vivo platforms are in phase I, their endpoints are safety and feasibility, and their most distinctive advantage so far is logistical rather than clinical — no apheresis, no weeks of manufacturing, and in one case no lymphodepletion. If you have a disease where an approved CAR-T already produces durable remissions, waiting converts a known benefit into an unknown one. The calculation changes only in specific situations: you cannot tolerate lymphodepletion, your T cells cannot be collected or manufactured, or your disease has no approved option and a trial is the alternative anyway.

The efficacy figures in the review are worth having in mind, though, because they show what the technology can do when the match is right. In relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, CD19 CAR-T produces complete responses in roughly 90% of patients. In aggressive B-cell lymphoma the figure falls to 40–54%. In heavily pretreated multiple myeloma, cilta-cel achieves strict complete response in 67%. Move the same therapy earlier and the gap widens further: in KarMMa-3, ide-cel produced complete responses in 39% of patients against 5% on standard regimens; in CARTITUDE-4, cilta-cel reached 73.1% against 21.8%.

Its forecasts are appropriately modest. Logic gating is expected to widen the therapeutic window where no single safe antigen exists, especially in solid tumours, and to produce synergistic benefit if combined with epitope spreading and platforms that recruit endogenous immunity. Bispecific T-cell engagers, being off-the-shelf and pharmacologically controllable, will remain a complementary modality, with the division of labour between cell therapy and antibody therapy decided by clinical trials rather than by preference. In vivo generation could substantially widen access, provided potency is not lost and toxicity is not added.

They also demonstrated the limit. With CD3ζ alone as the signalling domain, activation was suboptimal and antitumour efficacy was limited. Cells could find their target and could not sustain the fight. In the first cancer trials, reported in 2006, this showed up as two distinct problems: a first-generation carbonic anhydrase IX construct in renal cell carcinoma produced on-target, off-tumour liver toxicity, and a first-generation folate receptor construct in ovarian cancer produced poor persistence. The field learned both lessons at once — that specificity is not the same as safety, and that a cell which cannot persist cannot help.

It is worth being precise about the distinction. CAR-T re-engineers a patient's own T cells into a living drug that hunts a specific target. Dendritic-cell therapy does not re-engineer T cells at all; it educates the patient's existing immune system by presenting tumour antigen through its natural gateway. Both are cellular immunotherapies, and both are advancing in China's clinical ecosystem, but they work through different steps of the same pathway. That is why a patient weighing options should know both exist, and why a centre's real strength is offering the right mechanism for the right tumour rather than a single branded approach.

CD19 became the gold standard for three reasons that have little to do with cancer. It sits at uniformly high density on B cells at every stage of development. Losing the entire normal B-cell compartment is clinically survivable and, in most patients, reversible with immunoglobulin replacement. And CD19 is not required for the malignant cell's survival — which means the tumour cannot simply downregulate it and walk away. The technical term in the review is a disposable lineage, and it is the reason CD19 CAR-T can be simultaneously very effective and reasonably safe. BCMA follows the same logic in myeloma, being almost exclusive to plasma cells.

After a life-threatening relapse, her physicians used CD19 CAR-T on a compassionate basis. The reported sequence is unusually detailed. CAR-T cell levels peaked on day 9 while circulating B cells disappeared. The patient stopped needing transfusions on day 7. Haemoglobin began rising from day 9 and reached the normal range after day 25. Platelets recovered slowly across eleven months to about half of normal. Antiphospholipid antibodies became undetectable, no venous thrombosis was observed, and the patient was discharged on day 10. CAR-T cells became undetectable by day 322, at which point new B cells reappeared. No cytokine release syndrome occurred.

The most consequential one already is. Satri-cel — Claudin18.2 directed, approved for gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma — is the first CAR-T approved anywhere for a solid tumour, and it is a Chinese-developed product. Beyond that, access depends on trials rather than approvals: allogeneic and multi-edited products, in vivo platforms, and logic-gated constructs are largely in investigator-initiated studies at major centres. For an international patient the practical question is not which design is most advanced in principle but which approved product or open trial matches your disease, your line of therapy and your fitness for lymphodepletion.

Dr Lu also gave the number that separates a good centre from an average one. Experienced hospitals, she said, have brought the rate of severe complications down to 10 percent or even below 5 percent. That figure is not a property of the drug. It is a property of the institution: whether there is a dedicated cell-therapy ward, whether tocilizumab and steroids are on hand and released without a pharmacy delay, whether there is an intensive care bed that can be occupied the same hour, and whether the nursing team has seen enough of these patients to recognise the syndrome before it escalates. A centre that treats a handful of cases a year cannot quote the same number.

The third generation is the clearest evidence for this. It was designed on an entirely reasonable premise — if one co-stimulatory domain helps, two should help more — and it did not work out that way. Constructs carrying both CD28 and 4-1BB eradicated large established tumours in mouse mesothelioma models. In patients, the generation lagged behind the second, with inconsistent preclinical-to-clinical translation, contested benefit in blood cancers, and added concern about cytokine toxicity and premature T cell exhaustion. The design was more powerful on paper and less useful in practice. That is the fact that should attach itself to every future claim about a higher generation.

Two findings in this section have direct implications for anyone planning treatment, and neither is about a drug. First, exposure to bendamustine before apheresis is associated with worse outcomes after CD19 CAR-T — an argument for collecting T cells early rather than after several lines of lymphodepleting therapy. Second, high tumour burden before infusion is associated with both worse survival and worse toxicity, a two-way relationship supported by a multicentre analysis of tisa-cel in paediatric and young adult B-ALL and by metabolic tumour volume analysis in axi-cel recipients. That is the evidential basis for moving CAR-T earlier, into MRD-positive and low-burden settings.

Two off-the-shelf products point at the next stage. MT026 targets IL-13Rα2 and uses CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out the endogenous T-cell receptor and HLA class I molecules, preventing graft-versus-host disease and host rejection respectively. Its phase I study, published in Nature Communications in January 2026, treated five patients with recurrent high-grade glioma and very short expected survival by intrathecal injection, and reported an objective response rate of 80 percent, comprising one complete and three partial responses, with no grade 3 or higher adverse events. Its successor MT027, aimed at B7-H3, has been cleared by the US FDA for a phase II study in recurrent glioblastoma.

The reason this history is worth a patient's attention is not nostalgia. It is that the field's habits are visible in it. The pattern of solving one failure and creating the next is not a sign that something is wrong; it is how a technology matures. What it does mean is that any single claim — a new generation, a new target, a new platform — should be read as a statement about one part of a system that has many parts. The parts that decide whether a particular person benefits are still the unglamorous ones: how much disease is present, how early the treatment arrives, whether the target sits on anything the body needs, and whether the team managing the first week has done it before.

The hepatocellular and neuroendocrine programmes both use a dominant-negative TGF-beta receptor II. The receptor binds TGF-beta in the microenvironment but cannot transmit its suppressive signal, so the cell absorbs the inhibition without obeying it. The renal programme uses a co-stimulation platform intended to activate host immune cells alongside the CAR-T cells themselves. The colorectal peritoneal programme polarises cells toward Th9 and Tc9 phenotypes, on the argument that these persist longer and exhaust less. And the colorectal liver programme engineers antigen-independent activation, so cells can proliferate without waiting for a target to present itself at sufficient density.

Largely, yes — which is why baseline assessment is not a formality. Severity tracks tumour burden at infusion, product characteristics and host state, and burden-adapted split dosing is used precisely because the first of those is modifiable. What is not fixed is the outcome: CRS is a multi-cell cascade in which the CAR-T cell is only the trigger, and interrupting the amplifier with IL-1 or IL-6 blockade reduces severity without necessarily reducing efficacy. Two things to know in advance are IEC-HS, which appears as CRS improves and does not respond to tocilizumab alone, and, for central nervous system tumours treated locally, TIAN, which mimics progression on imaging and is not ICANS.

First, is the approval full or conditional, and what must be delivered before the deadline? Second, does the announcement contain a baseline, a follow-up interval and a control group, or only the fact that a procedure happened and a patient went home? Third, does the quoted price include the procedure, the hospital stay, the management of toxicity and follow-up? Fourth, does local insurance coverage apply to a foreign patient at all? In China's CAR-T market the parallel facts are worth restating: nine products are approved, all for cancer indications, none is reimbursed by national insurance, and international patients normally pay the published product price plus hospital service costs.

The open questions are as clearly stated as the progress. Delivery has to avoid hepatocytes, hematopoietic stem cells and tumour cells — and the last of those has a precedent: in the ex vivo era, leukaemic B cells were inadvertently transduced with CAR, producing antigen masking. With integrating systems, accidental tumour transduction is a far more serious prospect. Expansion needs to be sufficient without becoming uncontrolled. The role of lymphodepletion has to be redefined, since excessive depletion removes the very T cells you intend to modify. And whether the multi-component programmes that solid tumours require can be delivered with adequate fidelity remains an open engineering problem.

On efficacy, the most productive recent interventions have been transcriptional. Forcing expression of FOXO1 holds cells in a less differentiated, memory-like state with better metabolic fitness under chronic stimulation. Overexpressing JUN counteracts the transcriptional remodelling that drives exhaustion. Deleting TOX, PRDM1 or NR4A1 produces cells resistant to terminal exhaustion. Metabolic reprogramming — through ACLY, PRODH2, PTPN2, the adenosine A1 receptor — improves mitochondrial fitness. And manufacturing conditions may matter as much as genetics: a product designed to preserve naive and stem-cell memory phenotypes produced clinical responses at one twenty-fifth of the conventional dose.

The general rule is that design must match the specific obstacle the disease presents. Overexpressing c-JUN improves killing at low antigen density, which is exactly what you want in a tumour and exactly what you do not want if the target is also present at low density on normal tissue — the same modification that rescues efficacy can amplify off-tumour risk. Constructs that drive a strong effector state suit rapid debulking and suit poorly any setting that requires long-term immune suppression. The number of plausible combinations has outgrown the ability to test them one at a time, which is why systematic approaches such as CRISPR screening are becoming a prerequisite rather than a convenience.

Armouring is the clearest double-edged sword in the review. Adding IL-15 to a GPC3 CAR-T increased expansion, intratumoural survival and activity — and increased CRS. A CD19 CAR-T engineered to secrete IL-18, given to patients who had progressed after a previous CD19 CAR-T, produced a three-month overall response rate of 81% and complete response rate of 52%, with mostly low-grade toxicity. But a PSMA CAR-T combined with a dominant-negative TGF-beta receptor in prostate cancer produced dose-limiting CRS and fatal neurotoxicity, and the programme was terminated. Enhancement amplifies inflammation as readily as it amplifies killing; controllability has to be built in at the same time, not added later.

The report gives four reasons and does not dress them up. The first is the personalisation itself: one batch, one patient, no economies of scale, and no way to overproduce in anticipation of demand. The second is manufacturing complexity, which in practice means a cleanroom, a viral or non-viral gene delivery step, and a release-testing panel that has to certify identity, purity, potency and sterility before anything is infused. The third is the cost of the clinical development programme, amortised over a patient population measured in hundreds rather than millions. The fourth is regulation and supply chain: chain-of-identity tracking, cryogenic shipping, and a hospital that can hold a bed and staff it.

The more substantial dataset belongs to IMC002, a Claudin18.2 product built on a single-domain VHH nanobody. In the phase I/IIa study, 16 patients with multi-line treatment failure received infusions with no dose-limiting toxicity, no grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome or neurotoxicity, and no treatment-related deaths. Among 15 evaluable patients the objective response rate was 66.7 percent, disease control 93.3 percent and median progression-free survival 7.0 months, with one complete response lasting beyond 48 weeks and one partial response progression-free at 60 weeks. IMC002 has since entered phase III, making it the first VHH-based CAR-T in the world to reach a phase III trial in a solid tumor.

The team combined three techniques — S-EPTS/LM-PCR, next-generation sequencing, and GENE-IS/LISA — to characterise where the lentiviral vector landed in patients' genomes, and reported that integration was polyclonal. In plain terms: the edited cells did not descend from one or a few progenitors that outgrew everything else. Clonal dominance is the pattern that would raise concern about insertional oncogenesis, and it was not the pattern observed. Given that CAR-positive T cell malignancies have now been reported after some commercial and investigational products, a polyclonal integration profile in a new delivery route is the kind of evidence that takes years to accumulate and can be lost by a single dominant clone.

One line in that table deserves separating out, because it is the most common error in market coverage. The United States figure is often written as seven plus one plus one, and then reported as nine cell therapies or, worse, as nine CAR-T products. They are not interchangeable. The TIL product is a tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy for advanced melanoma. The TCR-T product is a T-cell receptor therapy for synovial sarcoma. Both are engineered or expanded T-cell treatments for solid tumours, and both are genuine advances, but neither is a chimeric antigen receptor T cell. A patient with lymphoma cannot be switched onto either, and a brochure that lists them together is either careless or hoping you will not notice.

The patient had progressive, metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer with co-mutation of KRAS G12V and STK11, a subtype that resists chemotherapy and immunotherapy and carries a poor outlook. Standard first-line treatment with carboplatin, pemetrexed and pembrolizumab had already failed. After a single infusion of A2B694, the tumour reached complete response at day 90, the result was confirmed at day 180, and a day-190 PET-CT showed no evidence of disease. A local recurrence in the central nervous system appeared at day 243; after dexamethasone and gamma-knife radiosurgery, a later PET-CT showed no disease, and the twelve-month scan showed no new lesions. Across the study, no dose-limiting or serious toxicity was observed.

An IF-THEN gate, built on SynNotch, requires recognition of a primer antigen before the cell expresses a CAR against a second one. An AND gate, as in LINK-CAR, splits the activation machinery across two receptors so that full activation requires both antigens simultaneously. A NOT gate, such as Tmod, uses an inhibitory receptor that recognises HLA retained by normal tissue, so the cell stands down wherever healthy cells are present and fires only where tumour loss of heterozygosity has removed that brake. The validation of a CD93 NOT gate in acute myeloid leukaemia, where it protected endothelium, shows what these circuits are for: not making a good target better, but unlocking targets that were previously disqualified as unsafe.

Chinese adult diabetes prevalence is now about 12.4 percent, so the potential pool is large. But the risk model does not transfer unchanged. A large Chinese prospective study found that pancreatic cancer risk rises with longer diabetes duration, unlike the Western pattern in which the first years after diagnosis are the most dangerous. Only 36.7 percent of people with diabetes in China are aware of their diagnosis, which makes the idea of new-onset hard to define from records alone. And in a US prospective cohort, three-year risk after age 50 was 0.84 percent in white participants but 0.22 percent in Asian participants, less than a third as high. A Chinese ENDPAC would need recalibration against a local cohort, not a translated cutoff.

On 22 June 2026 China approved 恺力美 (satricabtagene autoleucel, satri-cel; development code CT041) for advanced gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma that is Claudin18.2-positive and HER2-negative, after at least two lines of treatment have failed. It is the first CAR-T product anywhere in the world approved for a solid tumour. Three days later, the oncology team led by Professor Liu Tianshu at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, collected the T cells of the first commercial solid-tumor CAR-T patient in the world. Public follow-up reports say the patient has now completed the infusion, that imaging shows the tumour lesions shrinking, and that his general condition is good; long-term disease control is still being followed.

Tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity occurs when CAR-T cells are delivered locally into central nervous system tumours, and it presents as pseudoprogression, oedema and mass effect. It is a different entity from ICANS, with a different mechanism and a different management algorithm. The GD2 experience in diffuse midline glioma makes the contrast concrete: intravenous high-dose delivery was limited by CRS, while intraventricular delivery had no dose-limiting toxicity but produced TIAN frequently, requiring its own monitoring protocol. For families reading scan reports after intraventricular therapy, the difference between "the tumour grew" and "the tumour is inflamed" is the difference between abandoning a working treatment and continuing it.

Liver cancer has its own flagship in Ori-C101, a GPC3-directed armored CAR-T. The BEACON phase Ib study reported at ASCO 2026 enrolled 19 patients with GPC3-positive advanced hepatocellular carcinoma after at least two systemic lines, 18 of them evaluable. Objective response rate was 50 percent, disease control 77.8 percent and median overall survival 14.4 months; in the third dose level the response rate reached 66.7 percent with disease control at 88.9 percent, and one patient remains in complete response beyond 20 months. The safety profile demands its own sentence: cytokine release syndrome occurred in every patient, grade 3 or above in 42.1 percent, the highest rate in this review. There was no neurotoxicity and no delayed toxicity in extended follow-up.

At ASCO 2026 the CT041-CG4006 investigators reported an extended follow-up of a cohort that received satri-cel as sequential therapy after first-line treatment. Five patients with Claudin18.2-positive advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer were enrolled, and they were a difficult group: 60 percent had diffuse-type histology, 80 percent had signet ring cells and 80 percent had peritoneal metastases. The confirmed objective response rate was 100 percent. Median progression-free survival measured from first-line treatment was 20.9 months and median overall survival 22.1 months, with no grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome, no neurotoxicity of any grade and no treatment-related deaths. Five patients produced those numbers. They are a hypothesis, not a benchmark.

Ovarian cancer data center on mesothelin. KT127 completed a phase I study in 11 patients with platinum-resistant advanced disease, reporting disease control of 80 percent, median progression-free survival of 84 days and median overall survival of 129 days. One lesion shrank by half at nine months and a nodal lesion by 70 percent over three months, with no dose-limiting toxicity, no cytokine release syndrome and no neurotoxicity. The survival figures are sobering and should be quoted alongside the response rate. A second product, UCMYM802, is prepared by mRNA electroporation and co-expresses LACO-Stim; in nine patients with advanced mesothelin-positive tumors, including ovarian, pancreatic and peritoneal mesothelioma, response rate was 28.6 percent with disease control at 57.1 percent.

The most conceptually interesting product is CARv3-TEAM-E, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2024. It targets EGFRvIII and simultaneously secretes a T-cell engaging antibody against wild-type EGFR, so one product covers two antigen forms and partly answers the problem of antigen loss. Three patients received a single intraventricular infusion with no grade 3 or higher events, and tumors shrank markedly within days. Those responses were short-lived, which led to repeat dosing in one case at day 37. The ASCO 2025 update added seven patients: no dose-limiting toxicity, best response of stable disease in five, and a 33 percent reduction in tumor diameter after two infusions in one. Two patients who did not receive lymphodepleting chemotherapy survived beyond 12 and 20 months.

The costimulatory domain sets the personality of the cell. CD28 pushes toward early expansion and effector differentiation, at the cost of faster exhaustion. 4-1BB produces a more memory-like state and longer persistence, and commercial CD19 products built on 4-1BB report lower rates of ICANS — though cross-product comparisons must be read cautiously, since more than the costimulation domain differs between them. The instructive anomaly is that first-generation CARs without any costimulatory domain failed almost everywhere, with one exception: GD2 in neuroblastoma, where a first-generation construct induced durable remissions confirmed at eighteen years of follow-up. A design that failed across a dozen diseases succeeded in one, because that one disease happened to reward what that design did well.

The clearest example is CART-EGFR-IL-13Rα2, a dual-target product given by intraventricular injection straight into the cerebrospinal fluid. The phase I study published in Nature Medicine in 2025 enrolled 18 patients with recurrent glioblastoma; 62 percent of evaluable patients showed tumor regression, and median overall survival had not been reached at a median follow-up of 8.1 months. Longer follow-up presented at ASCO 2026 put median overall survival at 12.0 months, with three patients alive beyond 18 months. Apart from one previously reported grade 1 persistent neurotoxicity, no delayed or off-target toxicity appeared, and transient neurological decline after infusion recovered quickly. A second infusion did not reproduce the fluctuation seen after the first, which suggests repeat dosing is feasible.

Dendritic cells take up, process and present antigen, then deliver that information together with co-stimulatory signals and cytokines to T cells. They are the reason a naive T cell becomes an effector cell capable of killing tumours, and why some of those effectors become long-lived memory cells that respond fast on re-exposure. By function, the family splits into classical dendritic cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells and monocyte-derived inflammatory dendritic cells. Classical type 1 dendritic cells are the most important for launching CD8-positive T-cell responses against tumours; type 2 mainly activate CD4-positive T cells; plasmacytoid cells are weaker at activating T cells but strong at producing type 1 interferon; and monocyte-derived cells, made in the lab from monocytes under GM-CSF and IL-4, drive inflammation and can also promote T-cell reactions.

Other routes to the same end are less elegant but real. Some targets are carried by the mutation itself: in H3K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, the mutation-driven epigenetic disruption makes GD2 uniformly expressed, and GD2 CAR-T given intravenously or into the ventricle produced significant tumour regression, including one durable complete response. In neuroblastoma, GD2-CART01 was tolerable, persisted beyond twelve months in 64% of patients, and produced five-year overall survival of 43% across the cohort and 68% in the dose-optimised group. Oncofetal antigens — GPC2, GPC3, CLDN6 — form a third category: expressed during development, silenced at birth, switched back on in cancer. And a fourth strategy stops targeting the tumour altogether and targets its accomplices, with TREM2 and FOLR2 directed at immunosuppressive macrophages and uPAR at tumour stroma.

This is where Chinese autoimmune CAR-T differs most from its Western counterpart, and the pipeline is now crowded with variations on the theme. Gracell's GC012F, a BCMA/CD19 dual-target product developed on a next-day manufacturing platform and now part of AstraZeneca, holds Chinese trial clearance across four indications including refractory lupus. Qihan's QT-019C is an allogeneic, gene-edited CD19/BCMA product with trial clearance from both the FDA and Chinese regulators for refractory lupus. Juventas has taken a CD19 product, HY001N, into registered trials for lupus nephritis and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. And CSPC's SYS6042, cleared for a lupus trial in August 2026, is not a cell product at all in the conventional sense: it delivers CAR mRNA by lipid nanoparticle so that the patient's own T cells become CAR-T cells in the body, a format whose entire selling point is a lower rate of exactly the complication this paper is about.

DLL3 has become the busiest target in small cell lung cancer. LB2102 targets DLL3 and co-expresses a TGF-beta receptor blocking protein, an attempt to disarm the immunosuppressive microenvironment rather than simply increase dose. In the phase I data reported at ASCO 2026, 20 patients with recurrent small cell lung cancer or large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma received a single infusion with no dose-limiting toxicity and low, manageable rates of cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity. Among 17 evaluable patients, the objective response rate was 18 percent with disease control at 76 percent, and the median duration of response was 208 days. At doses of 2 million cells per kilogram or above, the response rate rose to 27 percent and disease control to 91 percent, a clear dose-response relationship. A separate case report described one patient with extensive-stage disease who remained free of progression 12 months after infusion, with complete regression of the target lesion, a healed compression fracture and no need for pain medication.

Renal cell carcinoma is being pursued through CD70. The allogeneic product ALLO-316 treated 39 patients, 38 of them evaluable, with an objective response rate of 20 percent overall and 33 percent in those with high CD70 expression. Grade 3 or higher cytokine release syndrome occurred in 2 percent and there was no grade 3 or higher neurotoxicity, but three grade 5 events were reported. Those are the only fatal events in this review, and they belong in any discussion of benefit. A second program, UCL70802, is autologous and co-expresses a LACO-Stim costimulatory molecule; in six patients with metastatic clear cell disease there was no dose-limiting toxicity, cytokine release syndrome was grade 1 to 2 in four and grade 3 in two, recovering to grade 2 within a day. At the 2 million cells per kilogram level, two of three patients reached partial response and one had confirmed shrinkage of 68.9 percent. One low-dose patient with low CAR-T exposure nonetheless had shrinkage lasting beyond six months, which hints that the LACO-Stim molecule may be activating endogenous antitumor immunity.

Colorectal cancer is being approached from three angles at once. For metastatic disease, a GUCY2C-directed phase I trial enrolled 20 patients with no dose-limiting toxicity during dose escalation; overall response rate was 26.3 percent, all responses occurred at higher dose levels, the third dose level reached 40 percent with median progression-free survival of 7.0 months, and patients with high GUCY2C expression reached 50 percent with 9.0 months. The cost was gastrointestinal: 55 percent had grade 3 diarrhea. In the adjuvant setting after curative resection of colorectal liver metastases, a CEA-directed study treated 12 patients with no serious adverse events, and 57.1 percent of the high-dose group remained recurrence-free at two years. For peritoneal metastases, a rapidly manufactured interleukin-9-secreting CAR-T aimed at CEACAM5 produced a response rate of 57.1 percent, disease control of 100 percent and maximum tumor shrinkage of 85.6 percent in 14 evaluable patients. And PC13, a hypoxia-responsive CEA product published in Nature Cancer in 2026, treated 43 patients with multi-line CEA-positive solid tumors through both intraperitoneal and intravenous routes, reaching disease control of 82.4 percent intraperitoneally and a response rate of 57.1 percent in CEA-high peritoneal disease.
